ask: Why is it on the path?
cards: For some 14,000 years the people of the Japanese archipelago lived mainly by hunting, gathering and fishing, and they made the world’s oldest known pottery around 14,500 BCE.
Hunter-gatherers of the Levant who lived in settled villages, some with round stone houses and the first known food stores, before farming began.
The earliest widely recognised culture of North America, mobile hunters of mammoth and bison with fluted stone points, though not the first people of the Americas.
Near the Bolan Pass, one of the earliest known places in South Asia where people farmed barley and wheat and herded sheep, goats and cattle.
It left the earliest known settlements on the southern Mesopotamian plain and the first temples there, but still no real cities: those came in the Uruk period.
Farmers between the Carpathians and the Dnieper who built some of the largest settlements in Eurasia, and burned and rebuilt them every 60 to 80 years.
Herders of the Pontic–Caspian steppe who moved in carts and wagons, buried their dead under mounds and are widely held to have spoken a stage of Proto-Indo-European.
Named after a drinking vessel shaped like an upside-down bell, it spread copper, gold and bronze working along sea and river routes from Portugal to Ireland and Hungary.
The salt mines of Hallstatt made its community unusually rich, and late in the period princely seats such as the Heuneburg traded with the Greek and Etruscan world.
The successor of Hallstatt from about 450 BCE, known for its curving metalwork and its walled oppida, many of which, such as Lutetia, became Roman cities.
